B. INTERNAL EDITORIAL RECORD — DO NOT PUBLISH

**Publication date:** 2026-10-04

**Title:** The presentation slide no one asked for: why AI summaries are making meetings longer

**Meta description:** AI tools make it trivial to turn documents into slides. Teams are discovering that automatic slides often extend meetings instead of clarifying thinking.

**Primary reader:** Presentation creator or meeting organiser choosing whether to use AI to generate slides from documents, and what to do with the output.

**Creative discipline:** Presentations and business content; presentation design practice and workflow.

**Platform or company, if relevant:** General practice; references to OpenAI and Microsoft Copilot capabilities.

**Central development or question:** AI presentation tools can automatically generate slide decks from source documents (reports, transcripts, notes). This capability is shifting how teams approach slide creation—but the ease of generation is creating a new problem: bloated decks that extend meetings rather than clarify decisions.

**Why readers will care:** Readers using or considering AI presentation tools need to understand that capability does not equal improvement. The article offers a framework for deciding when AI should generate slides and how to edit the output for actual meeting effectiveness.

**Most interesting supported detail:** Automated slide generation removes the friction that previously enforced editorial discipline. When slides took manual effort, scarcity ensured selectivity. Now, because generation is free and fast, teams are including everything—creating the inverse problem: dense, unfocused decks that turn meetings into information transfer sessions rather than decision-making forums.

**Central argument:** The ease of AI-generated slides obscures a more fundamental question: does this conversation need a slide deck at all? When slides are used, they should clarify a decision or narrative, not reproduce source material. Teams should use AI to draft and structure, then edit ruthlessly for the actual meeting purpose.

**Concrete takeaway:** Before using AI to generate slides from a document, ask: Does this meeting need a deck, or would a document, recording or focused five-slide narrative work better? If slides are needed, use AI to draft speaker notes or structure thinking, then edit the visual output to include only what moves the decision forward. Cut every slide that doesn't serve that purpose.

**Article format:** The considered opinion; a practical implication others have overlooked.

**Difference from the previous published article:** Previous article (2026-10-11) was a practical workflow check for presentation display and readability—tactical advice for a specific failure mode. This article addresses a broader practice question about how AI is reshaping presentation discipline and meeting effectiveness, questioning an assumed benefit rather than optimising an existing workflow.

**Closest related article in the supplied history and substantive difference:** The previous article is the only supplied history. No overlapping arguments. Previous article was tactical (how to check slide visibility); this is strategic (when and how to use AI for slide creation).

**Sources and relevant dates:** OpenAI and Microsoft Copilot presentation capabilities are documented in provided source headlines (ChatGPT office suite expansion, Copilot PowerPoint features noted in Computerworld source). No specific launch dates needed; the capability is established and spreading. The observation about meeting length and decision clarity is framed as a predictable consequence of the technology, not a cited study.

**Material availability restrictions:** None. The capability is widely available.

**Interpretation or prediction requiring qualification:** The claim that "more slides often extend meetings" is framed as an emerging observation, not a quantified finding. The article is cautious about causation—AI tools enable the behaviour; organisational discipline is required to prevent it.

**Research or history limitations:** No new research data supplied. The argument is built from observable patterns in how technology adoption changes behaviour, and from the practical reality that content density affects meeting effectiveness. The article does not claim to be reporting a study.

**Final reader-facing word count:** 368 words (including title, all body text, and source label).

**Estimated reading time at 200 words per minute:** 1 minute 50 seconds.

**Status:** READY

**Useful future angles:** 
- How to repurpose a presentation as a written narrative (or vice versa) without treating one as a simple conversion of the other.
- Why meeting recordings and asynchronous video summaries are replacing some live presentations.
- How design teams are handling brand consistency when AI generates slide layouts (relevant to toolbar use case).
- The economics of meeting time: what a 40-slide meeting actually costs an organisation.

**History summary:** Article examines how AI's ease of generating slides from documents is encouraging teams to include exhaustive content, creating longer, less focused meetings. The issue is not technical—AI can generate slides—but organisational: automatic capability removed the friction that previously enforced editorial discipline. The takeaway: use AI for drafting and structure, then edit ruthlessly for the actual meeting purpose. Useful for presentation creators deciding whether and how to use AI tools.
